newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Telecom CEO critical of NZ govt's economic policy.
newsitem.headline: Telecom CEO critical of NZ govt's economic policy.

text.p: Chief executive of New Zealand's largest company, Telcom Corp's Roderick Deane, on Friday took a swipe at the government's handling of the economy, saying it was not fully aware of the consequences of the economic slowdown.
"I really don't think that the government is fully aware of the extent of the slowdown in the economy and of the slowdown in corporate earnings," Deane told Reuters in an interview.
"Fletcher Challenge, Brierleys, Carter Holt, Lion, Air New Zealand have all had large drops in earnings, typically of the order of 20 to 50 percent.
"That means there'll be large drops in the tax take; that means the budget surplus will be lower; that means economic activity will be slower and unemployment will rise," he said.
Telecom, New Zealand's largest listed company, this week posted an annual profit of NZ$581.4 million, down from $716.8 million a year earlier.
While much of the decline was due to large one-off provisions, the phone utility's normalised earnings growth rate fell from 19.5 percent in 1995/96 to just 3.2 percent in 96/97.

Deane said Telecom's profit growth was linked to economic growth. "Slower growth rates in earnings are a product partly of the economy, which is growing at less than half the rate it was a year or two ago," he said.
New Zealand's GDP growth was 2.7 percent in December 1996, down from 3.5 percent in 1995.
Deane stressed he was not blaming his company's fall in earnings growth on the government, but said the tight rein it was keeping on the economy raised important questions.

"It does raise real questions, given how low the inflation rate is at the moment, about whether the combination of fiscal surplus and the very tight monetary policy...is actually tighter than is really needed in order to keep the economy moving and to keep unemployment down," he said.
"The cheapest way to keep unemployment down is economic growth, not handing out unemployment benefits, which we're going to have to start doing at an increased rate again."
Deane said he had been enormously supportive of government's economic policy in the past.

"I think it's been very responsible, so I wouldn't want to suggest that it's significantly astray, but I think it has got to the point now where...you've got to say to yourself, 'is it a bit on the tight side?' I think it is.
"And that's the first time that I've said that in a decade."
However, Deane, a former Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank, commended current Governor Don Brash for a "splendid job", and rejected speculation that he might one day be interested in the position.

"Don Brash is doing a fantastic job. Why would I want to replace somebody who is doing such a splendid job? I think he's been brilliant in that job. Moreover, I don't think anybody would offer it to me."
